analysis.one_liner: Restores individuals' and small businesses' right to sue in court instead of forced arbitration.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Senator Leahy with 17 Democratic cosponsors, the bill died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies routinely put fine-print clauses into consumer, employment, and small-business contracts that force any dispute into private arbitration instead of court. Court decisions like AT&T Mobility v. Concepcion have let those clauses wipe out rights Congress and the states created — like joining a class action. This bill would invalidate those clauses when an individual or small business is trying to enforce a federal or state law, the U.S. Constitution, or a state constitution, letting them take those claims to a real court instead. The Senate Judiciary Committee never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Individuals and small businesses with legal claims under federal or state statutes, the U.S. Constitution, or state constitutions. They could no longer be forced into private arbitration by a contract they signed before a dispute arose, and a court — not a private arbitrator — would decide whether an arbitration agreement is enforceable. Claims covered include consumer protection, employment, and civil rights statutes.

how_it_helps.text: Invalidate pre-dispute arbitration clauses for claims by individuals or small businesses arising from alleged violations of federal or state statutes, the U.S. Constitution, or state constitutions, restoring access to courts.
Preserve arbitration only when both parties agree after a claim has arisen and the agreement covers solely that existing claim — so genuinely voluntary arbitration remains available.
Let state laws against unconscionable or otherwise unenforceable arbitration agreements count as grounds to void a contract, restoring states' ability to police forced arbitration.
Require a court, not an arbitrator, to decide whether an arbitration agreement is enforceable, closing a common maneuver of sending even that question into private arbitration.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that embed mandatory arbitration clauses in consumer, employment, and small-business contracts — banks and credit card issuers, telecom and cable companies, employers, nursing homes, and other consumer-facing firms — would lose a legal shield: they would face more individual lawsuits and class actions in court, with public proceedings and jury verdicts. Arbitration providers would see fewer forced consumer cases.

drawbacks.text: The bill is narrower than a full ban on forced arbitration: arbitration agreements remain valid for purely commercial disputes between sophisticated parties, and it applies only to claims arising after enactment.

Businesses argue that arbitration resolves disputes faster and more cheaply for consumers than court, and that class actions raise costs that get passed through to all customers in the form of higher prices; this bill would push many more disputes into litigation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is clear: companies give up a procedural system they chose for themselves, and individuals and small businesses get back the courtroom rights Congress and state legislatures wrote into law. The bill is carefully drawn — voluntary post-dispute arbitration stays legal and sophisticated commercial parties are untouched — but the cost of moving disputes from arbitration into court is real: litigation is slower and more expensive per case, and businesses contend consumers ultimately share those costs. Weighing it, the main benefit (millions of people being able to actually enforce statutory rights) outweighs the efficiency costs, but the design is a partial fix, not a cure.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Leahy introduced it with four Democratic colleagues on February 4, 2016, but the Senate Judiciary Committee never held a hearing or a vote, and the bill died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Leahy introduced the bill on February 4, 2016, along with original cosponsors Senators Franken, Blumenthal, Durbin, and Whitehouse, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
Seventeen additional Democratic senators later signed on as cosponsors; no Republican did.
The only action ever taken on the bill was the February 4 referral to the Judiciary Committee; it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that write mandatory arbitration clauses into consumer, employment, and small-business contracts came out ahead: without this law, they keep the ability to route claims under federal and state statutes into private arbitration and away from courts and class actions. Consumers, workers, and small businesses are left with the same diminished access to court the bill aimed to restore.

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and guided its referral to the Judiciary Committee.

for.name: Sens. Franken, Blumenthal, Durbin, and Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote during the 114th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 5 original sponsors and all 17 additional cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican signed on; there is no record of any floor vote where party breakdowns would appear.

industries.industry: Banks, credit card issuers, telecoms, and other consumer-facing businesses
industries.note: These companies' contracts routinely force consumer disputes into private arbitration, where the bill would bar pre-dispute clauses for statutory claims. Their arbitration advantage — avoiding courts, juries, and class actions — comes directly at the cost of ordinary people's ability to enforce their rights.

Employee claims under labor and civil rights statutes could no longer be forced into pre-dispute arbitration, exposing employers to public court proceedings. Workers would regain the forum Congress's employment laws envisioned.

Private arbitration firms earn fees from disputes companies force consumers and employees into; the bill would shrink that caseload for statutory claims while leaving genuinely voluntary post-dispute arbitration intact.
Trial lawyers would gain a larger docket of court cases as statutory claims move out of arbitration; their gain runs alongside the public's restored access to courts.
